unverified.claim: Across 59 studies (238 effect sizes, 158 samples), interleaved presentation produced a moderate overall benefit over blocked presentation for inductive learning (Hedges' g = 0.42).

The interleaving advantage is domain-dependent: strong for visual category learning (paintings g = 0.67, naturalistic photographs g = 0.35), small for mathematical tasks (g = 0.34), nonsignificant for expository texts, and reversed (blocking superior) for words (g = -0.39) — directly bearing on whether contextual interference generalizes to verbal/conceptual materials like law.

Consistent with the discriminative contrast / attentional bias account, the interleaving effect increased with between-category similarity and material complexity, and decreased with within-category similarity — i.e., interleaving pays off when categories are hard to discriminate, blocking when categories are easily discriminable but exemplars within a category are dissimilar.

The authors explicitly caution against applying interleaving to text-based and verbal educational materials (expository texts, grammar rules, foreign languages, word/category names) and even mathematical tasks, warning it could impair learning relative to blocking — a key qualification for a law-study drill built on expository/verbal content.

The interleaving advantage operates via discriminative contrast: interleaved sequencing helps learners detect predictive differences between easily confusable categories, which is the mechanism required for distinguishing similar categories (directly supports the condition that interleaving pays off when items are similar/confusable, e.g., adjacent legal doctrines).

Interleaving's advantage over blocking is conditional on between-category similarity: when categories are highly distinct and share almost no features, interleaving is expected to be relatively disadvantageous compared to blocking — supporting a design rule of interleaving confusable topics but not necessarily unrelated ones.

Directly manipulating the opportunity for discriminative contrast (Experiment 3) showed a dose-response effect: higher-contrast presentation produced significantly better category induction than medium- and low-contrast conditions, supporting the discriminative-contrast hypothesis as the mechanism of the interleaving effect.

The authors identify material type as a moderator of which mechanism dominates: visual materials benefit mainly from discriminative contrast (favoring interleaving of confusable categories), whereas expository text materials benefit mainly from distributed practice (spacing) — directly relevant to whether the interleaving advantage generalizes to verbal/conceptual domains like law.
인터리빙과 블로킹의 상대적 효과는 범주 간 유사성에 따라 갈린다: 고유사성 범주(구별이 어려운 자료)는 인터리빙이 범주 간 비교를 촉진해 학습을 향상시키고, 저유사성 범주는 블로킹이 범주 내 비교를 촉진해 학습을 향상시킨다 — discriminative contrast(변별 대비) 조건 가설을 직접 지지한다.
학습 스케줄(인터리빙 vs 블로킹)과 범주 유형(고/저 유사성) 간에 통계적으로 유의한 상호작용이 확인되었다(F(1,111)=4.26, p=0.04, 참가자 113명 피험자내 설계).
24시간 지연 검사에서도 이 상호작용 패턴은 즉시 검사와 동일하게 유지되었으며, 파지 간격을 늘려도 인터리빙의 이점이 추가로 커지지 않았다 — 즉 인터리빙 이점이 지연 후에야 나타난다는 주장(장기기억에서만 우세)을 이 자료 유형에서는 지지하지 않는다.
인터리빙의 이점은 주로 시간적 분산(spacing) 때문이 아니라 인터리빙이 촉진하는 범주 간 비교(cross-category comparison) 때문이라고 저자들은 결론짓는다 — 이는 인터리빙 효과의 기제가 '대비를 통한 변별 학습'임을 시사하며, 유사 쟁점 간 혼동이 큰 과제일수록 인터리빙이 유리하다는 설계 함의를 준다.

In inductive category learning (259 participants classifying paintings by six artists), both random and adaptive interleaved schedules produced better learning outcomes than blocked practice on both an immediate and a delayed test — supporting interleaving (structure A) over topic-blocked clustering (structure B) for retention when the task requires discriminating between confusable categories.

Blocked practice produced better performance and higher category learning judgments during the study phase, and interleaved study lowered learners' category learning judgments — i.e., blocking creates a metacognitive illusion of learning: acquisition-phase fluency and confidence favor blocking even though delayed retention favors interleaving.

Across four experiments (293+ college students and adult learners), interleaved practice of two Romance-language grammatical tenses produced better performance than blocked practice on a one-week delayed criterial test: verb conjugation improved in all four experiments, tense identification in Experiments 1 and 3, and language identification in Experiment 4 — supporting interleaving (A) over topic-blocked sequencing (B) for long-term retention of rule-based verbal material.

The interleaving benefit for the multi-step procedural skill (verb conjugation) did NOT depend on between-category similarity — it appeared even for highly dissimilar, easily distinguishable tenses — which the authors attribute to strengthened problem-type-to-procedure associations (as in math interleaving) rather than discriminative contrast; this suggests the contextual-interference benefit generalizes to non-perceptual, rule/procedure-based tasks like legal rule application.

The discriminative-contrast condition (angle 1): for category-identification tasks, interleaving helped only when the categories were confusable — in Experiment 2, where the two tenses were highly dissimilar and easy to tell apart, interleaving showed no benefit for tense identification — implying interleaving pays off most when the mixed items are similar enough to be confused (e.g., confusable legal issues), not for trivially distinguishable topics.

For novices, instruction based on worked examples only (WE) and example-problem pairs (WE-PS) produced lower cognitive load during learning and higher learning outcomes than problem solving only (PS) — supporting concept/example-first sequencing for low-expertise learners.

Sequence order matters: problem-example pairs (problem first, then example) were no more effective than problem solving only, so when alternating study and practice, the example/concept should come before the problem.

The expertise reversal effect — instructional techniques effective for low-knowledge learners losing effectiveness or becoming harmful for more proficient learners — is consistently replicated across many domains and over 2200 participants, with conservative effect-size differences ranging from 0.45 to 2.99 (mid-range 1.72).

The superiority of worked examples over problem solving holds only for less knowledgeable learners and reverses with expertise: in Kalyuga and Sweller (2004, Experiment 3) less knowledgeable high-school students benefited significantly more from worked examples while more knowledgeable learners showed clear problem-solving benefits, with a significant knowledge-by-format interaction.

Reisslein et al. (2006), in electrical circuit analysis with university engineering students, found that novices learned more from example-problem pairs (worked example first, then isomorphic problem), whereas higher-prior-knowledge learners learned more from problem-example pairs and backward-faded worked example sequences.

The optimal pace of fading from worked examples to independent problem solving depends on prior knowledge: Reisslein (2005) found low-prior-knowledge learners retained more under slow backward fading, while more knowledgeable learners performed significantly better under fast or immediate transitioning to problem solving.
Worked examples are an effective complement to tutored problem solving, and prior research supports combining example study with problem-solving practice rather than problem solving alone.
